title: Boxing and hidden allocations
description: Learn how boxing allocates memory on the heap, identify common hidden allocation patterns, and eliminate unnecessary GC pressure.

data.text: Boxing is one of the most common sources of hidden allocations in C# code. It happens whenever a value type — a `struct`, an `int`, a `bool` — is cast to `object` or to an interface type the struct implements. At that moment, the runtime allocates a new object on the managed heap, copies the value inside it, and returns a reference to the heap object. This allocation is invisible in your source code, which makes it easy to introduce accidentally in performance-sensitive paths.

The reverse operation — unboxing — extracts the value type from the heap object. Unboxing is cheap: it reads a pointer and returns the value. But unboxing to a value type and then re-boxing it creates two heap allocations where zero were needed. In tight loops or frequently called methods, these hidden allocations can dominate your GC pressure and slow down your application without any obvious smoking gun.

When you write `object o = 42;`, the runtime performs three steps: it allocates a new object on the heap with the size of the boxed type plus the object header, it copies the value `42` into the object's data field, and it returns an `object` reference pointing to the heap object. The boxed object carries a type pointer so the runtime knows what type is inside. You can unbox it with `(int)o`, which reads the value without further allocation.

data.title: Boxing and its hidden cost

data.text: Boxing is the most well-known hidden allocation, but it is not the only one. String concatenation in loops allocates a new string on every iteration. `nameof()` does not allocate, but string interpolation with non-string values does. `Guid.NewGuid()` allocates a 16-byte struct on the heap when boxed. `DateTime.UtcNow` returns a value type, but putting it in a non-generic collection boxes it. The pattern is always the same: a value type crosses a boundary that requires a reference type, and the runtime allocates to bridge the gap.

data.title: Finding hidden allocations with a benchmark

data.text: Eliminating boxing with generics and ReadOnlySpan<char>

The `where T : struct` constraint on generic methods tells the compiler that `T` is a value type. When the compiler sees `T` used in a generic context, it generates code that keeps `T` as a value type — no boxing. Similarly, `ReadOnlySpan<char>` replaces `string` in many parsing and comparison scenarios without allocating. The `string.Create` API introduced in .NET 6 builds strings without intermediate allocations by formatting directly into the final buffer.

data.title: Generic method avoiding boxing
Use BenchmarkDotNet to find boxing hotspots
data.text: Boxing allocations are often invisible until you profile them. Run your code through BenchmarkDotNet with the `MemoryDiagnoser` attribute. It will report the number of allocations per operation. Look for any benchmark with more than 0 bytes allocated in a method that should be allocation-free. If a hot path is boxing, refactoring it to use generics or spans can eliminate thousands of allocations per second.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: Boxing wraps a value type in a heap-allocated object whenever it is cast to `object` or a non-generic interface.
String concatenation in loops, non-generic collections, and interface dispatch are common hidden allocation sources.
`where T : struct` keeps value types unboxed in generic methods; prefer `IComparable<T>` over `IComparable`.
`ReadOnlySpan<char>` and `string.Create` eliminate intermediate allocations in string-heavy parsing.
